title: Who Owns Sharper Image Now? No Stores Since 2008
body:
Sharper Image is owned by ThreeSixty Group, a consumer products company in Irvine, California that bought the brand from Iconix Brand Group for $100 million in December 2016 and still holds it in 2026. The retail chain itself is gone: Sharper Image filed for Chapter 11 in February 2008 and its assets were auctioned for $49 million that May. What is left is a website, a catalog and a licensing program, not a store you can walk into.

Quick facts
Peak revenue
$760.0 million in fiscal 2004, the year ended January 31, 2005
Bankruptcy
Chapter 11 in February 2008; assets auctioned for $49 million in May 2008
Owner today
ThreeSixty Group of Irvine, California, which paid $100 million in December 2016
Stores left
None in the United States; the last retail space was a 2017 Times Square pop-up
Status today
A licensed brand selling through sharperimage.com, a catalog and other retailers, with the Axis 4D massage chair listed at $6,999 in 2026

How big was Sharper Image before the collapse?

Sharper Image spent the early 2000s as one of the most recognizable names in an American mall: massage chairs, air purifiers, chrome desk toys and whatever gadget the catalog was pushing that season.

The business peaked in fiscal 2004. Sharper Image reported revenues of $760.0 million for the year ended January 31, 2005, split between its stores, its printed catalog and its website.

That was the high point. Revenue slid in the years that followed, the company cycled through leadership, and the single product that had carried the growth became the liability that ended it.

The timing invites filing the decline alongside the 2008 retail wipeout that also took Circuit City. That is not what happened here. Sharper Image's trouble started six years earlier, with one air purifier, and it was already visible in the numbers before the recession arrived.

What did the Ionic Breeze cost Sharper Image?

The Ionic Breeze was a tall, silent, filterless air purifier, and for several years it was the product Sharper Image moved more of than anything else on the sales floor.

It sold in enormous numbers. CBS News reported in January 2007 that the class in a settled consumer lawsuit over the machine covered roughly 3.2 million people who had bought one since May 6, 1999.

The terms were expensive. Sharper Image signed the settlement on January 16, 2007 in the US District Court for the Southern District of Florida, agreed to more than $60 million in discounts on its merchandise, offered each of those buyers a $19 credit good for a year, and agreed to pay up to $1.875 million to the lawyers who brought the case.

The allegation at the center of it was that the Ionic Breeze did not clean air the way the advertising said it did, and that it emitted ozone. A $19 credit does not repair that. The product that had built the company had become the reason shoppers stopped trusting it.

Why did suing Consumer Reports backfire?

Consumer Reports tested the Ionic Breeze and was blunt about it. The magazine told readers in its February 2002 and October 2003 issues that the machine delivered "almost no measurable reduction in airborne particles."

Sharper Image sued the magazine's publisher, Consumers Union, in September 2003, arguing the reviews were false.

It lost. In November 2004 the US District Court for the Northern District of California threw the case out under California's anti-SLAPP statute. Judge Maxine Chesney found that Sharper Image "has not demonstrated a reasonable probability that any of the challenged statements were false," and that it had not shown the magazine's test protocol was invalid.

Then came the bill. Consumers Union collected $525,000 in legal fees and costs early in 2005. The suit did what suits against reviewers usually do: it pushed the review back into the news and welded the company's name to it permanently.

What happened at the 2008 bankruptcy auction?

Sharper Image filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in February 2008 from its San Francisco headquarters.

No reorganization followed. The company's assets went to a bankruptcy auction in New York on May 28, 2008, and a joint venture led by units of Hilco Consumer Capital, Gordon Brothers Group, Infinity Lifestyle Brands and Bluestar Alliance won it with a bid of $49 million.

That number is the story in one line. A retailer that had booked $760.0 million in revenue four years earlier changed hands for $49 million, and what the buyers wanted was not the shops.

The group said it had a global licensing strategy ready for wholesale, retail, direct-to-retail, ecommerce and catalog business. In practice the name would be rented out and the stores would not reopen, the same route RadioShack took a few years later.

How did ThreeSixty Group end up with the name?

Trademarks that pass through liquidators rarely stay put, and this one moved twice more.

The Sharper Image mark ended up with Iconix Brand Group, a company whose business is collecting names and licensing them out. ThreeSixty Group, a consumer products manufacturer in Irvine, California, had been licensing Sharper Image products since 2008 and had grown into the brand's largest licensee.

In December 2016 the tenant bought the building. ThreeSixty Group acquired the Sharper Image brand and its intellectual property from Iconix Brand Group for $100 million, in a deal that closed on December 30, 2016. Behind ThreeSixty sits the private investment firm AEA Investors, which took a majority position in the company in 2015.

ThreeSixty also owns FAO Schwarz, bought the same year, which says a good deal about how it reads the category: a famous retail name, no retail required. Nothing has changed hands since, and ThreeSixty Group still holds Sharper Image in 2026.

Can you shop at a Sharper Image store in 2026?

Not in a store. There are no Sharper Image retail locations operating in the United States in 2026, and there have been none since the 2008 liquidation emptied the chain.

There was one attempt at a return. ThreeSixty opened a two-story Sharper Image pop-up at 4 Times Square for the 2017 holidays, the brand's first retail space in a decade, and closed it in the middle of January. "We wanted a lot of room to do product demos," ThreeSixty Brands chief executive David Conn told PYMNTS in 2017, adding that "this is what's missing from retail today." A mall franchise program announced the following year produced no stores.

What survives is the name and the channels behind it: sharperimage.com, a printed catalog, and licensees including Conair, Vornado Air and Aerus whose goods reach shoppers through other retailers. The product mix is recognizable enough, air purifiers, massagers, heated pillows, remote-control toys, and the prices are not nostalgic: the Sharper Image Axis 4D massage chair listed at $6,999 across its dealer network in October 2026. What is missing is the demonstration, which was the whole reason the chain worked. The Segway hit the same wall.

Where to find one today. Original Sharper Image gear lives in the collector market rather than at retail. In October 2026, vintage Sharper Image catalogs from the early 1980s ran about $7 to $35, with a Summer 1983 issue listed at $20, and desk gadgets and air purifier towers sitting above that. Browsing the vintage Sharper Image listings on Etsy is the practical way to see what is actually circulating.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who owns Sharper Image now?

Sharper Image is owned by ThreeSixty Group, a consumer products company in Irvine, California that bought the brand and its intellectual property from Iconix Brand Group for $100 million in a deal closing on December 30, 2016. ThreeSixty had licensed Sharper Image products since 2008, and the private investment firm AEA Investors took a majority position in ThreeSixty in 2015.

Is Sharper Image still in business?

Sharper Image still exists as a brand in 2026, but not as a store chain. The retailer filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in February 2008 and its assets were auctioned that May, and since then Sharper Image has run as a website, a catalog and a licensing program rather than a company with shops of its own.

What happened to the Ionic Breeze air purifier?

The Ionic Breeze was Sharper Image's best-selling product and the source of its worst publicity. Consumer Reports found in 2002 and 2003 that it barely reduced airborne particles, Sharper Image sued the magazine's publisher in September 2003 and lost in November 2004, and a January 2007 settlement gave roughly 3.2 million buyers a $19 merchandise credit.
